items.title: 3.3.3 Applications of the VSEPR model in drug designing

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.3, printed pages 58-59. Figure 3.21 (aspirin bound to COX, a published image) is not reproduced; the text carries the example.

blocks.text: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose or treat a disease. They interact with the human body at specific points, or with specific processes, called targets or substrates, through their bioactive molecules called ligands. A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand through binding; examples of targets in the body are receptors such as enzymes, proteins, nucleic acids and cellular pathways. Each drug interacts with a specific target to a different degree, a feature called the specificity of the drug or ligand.

blocks.alt: Lock-and-key scheme. Two keys, A and B, above a block labelled Receptor whose notch matches key A. Below: 'Drug A binds to receptor' and 'Drug B cannot bind to receptor'.
blocks.caption: Drug A binds to the receptor; drug B cannot bind to the receptor (original drawing after the lock-and-key scheme printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: Molecular shape is an important feature that determines how a drug interacts with a biological target: only ligands with a suitable shape can fit the active sites of a target, as a specific key fits a specific lock. The VSEPR model is successfully applied in determining the shapes of various biological systems, such as substrate recognition, ligand specificity or selectivity, and antibody recognition. For example, aspirin is an analgesic (painkiller) used as a primary medicine for relief from pain. It interacts with the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) by binding to its active site through its acetyl group, -OCCH3. The shape of the COX active site and that of the acetyl group on aspirin are compatible, so the binding succeeds and blocks COX, which is a cause of pain in the body.

blocks.alt: Two green enzyme units side by side in a lipid membrane, labelled 'Platelet COX-1 dimer'. In the left unit a red dot marked 'Ser' carries a red acetyl group (O=C-CH3), with the label 'irreversible acetylation' over a red bracket. A solid arrow runs from aspirin (a benzene ring with COOH and a red O-CO-CH3 group) up into the channel, and a dashed arrow runs out to salicylic acid (a benzene ring with COOH and OH).
